title: Spacing Semantics — Inset, Stack, Inline, and Gap
content:
A spacing SCALE gives you legal values. Spacing SEMANTICS gives those values names that say what they are for, which is what makes a spacing token self-documenting and reviewable.

THE FOUR RELATIONAL CATEGORIES:
- INSET — padding inside a container. `space/inset/md`. The space between a box's edge and its content.
- STACK — vertical space between stacked siblings. `space/stack/sm`. Governs vertical rhythm.
- INLINE — horizontal space between inline siblings. `space/inline/xs`. Icon-to-label, chip-to-chip, breadcrumb separators.
- GAP — space between items in a grid or flex layout where direction is set by the container. `space/gap/lg`.

INSET VARIANTS, which are the part most systems miss:
- INSET SQUISH — less vertical than horizontal. `inset-squish/md` = 8px top/bottom, 16px left/right. This is the correct shape for buttons, chips, tags, and table cells; equal padding on a button always looks bottom-heavy and too tall.
- INSET STRETCH — more vertical than horizontal. Rare; used for tall list rows and some cards.
- INSET SQUARE — equal on all sides. Cards, modals, panels.

WHY THIS IS WORTH THE MIGRATION: `padding: var(--space-4)` tells a reviewer nothing. `padding: var(--space-inset-squish-md)` says "this is a control, and its padding is deliberately asymmetric". It also makes density modes trivial — a compact mode remaps the semantic names one step down rather than hunting every raw value.

MAPPING TO FIGMA: inset → auto layout padding; stack → vertical auto layout item spacing; inline → horizontal auto layout item spacing; gap → grid layout gap. Scope each variable to only the property it belongs to (see ds-021, ds-022) so the picker offers stack values for vertical gaps and nothing else.

THE PROXIMITY RULE STILL GOVERNS: inset < stack within a group < stack between groups, with at least a 1.5x step so the difference is perceptible.
source: Atlassian Design System / Adobe Spectrum spacing taxonomy; Infrasity-Labs/dev-gtm-claude-skills (MIT) — spacing-system

title: Icon System — Grid, Keylines, Stroke, and Optical Correction
content:
An icon set without a grid is a collection of drawings. The grid is what makes forty icons look like one family.

THE CANVAS: a 24x24px artboard with a 20x20px LIVE AREA — 2px of padding on all sides that no artwork enters. The padding is what stops icons from touching each other and their labels, and it is why a 24px icon reads as smaller than 24px.

KEYLINE SHAPES — every icon should resolve to one of these so optical weight stays constant:
- Square: 18x18
- Circle: 20x20 diameter
- Vertical rectangle: 16 wide x 20 tall
- Horizontal rectangle: 20 wide x 16 tall
A square and a circle of identical pixel dimensions look different sizes; the circle must be larger to appear equal. That is the entire reason keylines exist.

STROKE: 1.5px or 2px at the 24px base. 1.5px reads as refined and modern; 2px reads as sturdier and survives small sizes better. Pick one and never mix — mixed stroke weight is the single most visible inconsistency in an icon set.

CORNER RADIUS: one value for outer corners (commonly 2px at 24px) and one for inner joins. Terminals either all rounded or all butt — not both.

OPTICAL CORRECTION — the rule people get wrong: an icon drawn at 24px and scaled to 16px has a stroke of 1px, which renders thin and grey. A true 16px icon needs its stroke redrawn at 1.5px and its detail simplified, not scaled. Two or three optical sizes (16, 20/24, 32) drawn separately beats one set scaled everywhere.

PIXEL ALIGNMENT: draw strokes on whole or half pixels at the base size. A 1.5px stroke centred on a whole-pixel path renders as a soft 2px smear.
source: Material Symbols and Apple SF Symbols grid specifications; Infrasity-Labs/dev-gtm-claude-skills (MIT) — icon-system

title: Icon System — Naming, Size Ramp, and Delivery
content:
NAMING — `icon/[category]/[name]/[variant]`, with variant covering style and state:
`icon/action/trash/outline`, `icon/action/trash/filled`, `icon/status/check-circle/filled`.
Categories that hold up: action, navigation, content, communication, social, status, file, device, media, commerce, crypto.
Name by MEANING, not by picture. `icon/action/delete` survives a redesign from a bin to an X; `icon/trash-can` does not. The exception is genuinely pictorial brand marks.

STYLE PAIRS: most systems need outline and filled for the same glyph, because filled communicates the selected/active state in tab bars and toggles. Ship them as a variant property on one component, not as two unrelated icons.

SIZE RAMP, bound to the icon token scale (see ds-040):
xs 12 · sm 16 · md 20 · lg 24 · xl 32 · 2xl 48
Note the split: 12 and 16 need their own optical drawings; 20 and 24 can share; 32 and 48 can share.

TOUCH TARGET IS NOT ICON SIZE. A 16px icon still needs a 44x44pt (iOS) / 48x48dp (Android) target, achieved with a padded transparent parent. Enforce it in the component so a designer cannot ship a bare glyph as a button.

ACCESSIBILITY:
- Every icon is either labelled or explicitly decorative. Icon-only controls need an accessible name; decorative icons get `aria-hidden`.
- Icon-only for a critical or destructive action is a comprehension gamble. Pair with text, or accept a measurable error rate.
- Icons carry the same 3:1 contrast requirement as other non-text UI components.

DELIVERY: SVG source with strokes converted to outlines only at the final export step (keep editable strokes in the library), a Figma component set with a size property and a colour variable bound to `icon/default`, and a code wrapper that takes size and colour as props rather than shipping pre-coloured files.

GOVERNANCE: a contribution route, a rejection criterion, and a quarterly pass to delete unused icons. Icon sets grow monotonically unless someone is allowed to say no.

title: Layering — A Z-Index Token Scale
content:
Ad-hoc z-index values are one of the most reliable sources of production bugs: a dropdown behind a sticky header, a tooltip behind a modal, a toast that cannot be seen. It is a token problem and it is almost never tokenised.

THE SCALE — leave gaps so new layers can be inserted without renumbering:
| Token | Value | Layer |
|---|---|---|
| `z/base` | 0 | Normal document flow |
| `z/raised` | 10 | Cards and surfaces on hover, focused inputs |
| `z/sticky` | 100 | Sticky headers, sticky table headers, sticky filter bars |
| `z/dropdown` | 200 | Selects, menus, autocomplete, date pickers |
| `z/scrim` | 300 | The dim behind a modal or drawer |
| `z/modal` | 400 | Dialogs, drawers, bottom sheets |
| `z/popover` | 500 | Popovers anchored to modal content |
| `z/toast` | 600 | Snackbars and notifications — must clear modals |
| `z/tooltip` | 700 | Always on top; a tooltip is never obscured |

THE ORDERING DECISIONS WORTH MAKING EXPLICIT:
- Toast above modal. A confirmation or error that fires while a dialog is open must be visible, or the user is stuck.
- Tooltip above everything, including toast.
- Dropdown BELOW scrim, so opening a modal correctly covers an open menu.
- A popover launched from inside a modal needs its own level above the modal, which is why `z/popover` sits where it does.

THE GOTCHA THAT BREAKS THE SCALE: `z-index` only competes within its STACKING CONTEXT. `transform`, `filter`, `opacity` below 1, `will-change`, `backdrop-filter`, and `position: fixed` with a transform all create a new context. A child with `z/tooltip` inside a card that has `transform: translateY(...)` cannot escape that card, no matter how high the number. The fix is portalling the element to the document root, not raising the value — so this belongs in the handoff note, not just the token file.

FIGMA MAPPING: Figma has no z-index; layer order is the equivalent. Document the intended layer order in the component and state it in handoff, because canvas order does not survive translation on its own.

title: Border, Radius, and Focus-Ring Tokens
content:
RADIUS SCALE, and the rule that makes it look intentional:
`radius/none` 0 · `radius/sm` 4 · `radius/md` 8 · `radius/lg` 12 · `radius/xl` 16 · `radius/2xl` 24 · `radius/full` 9999
NESTED RADIUS RULE: an inner element's radius should be the outer radius minus the padding between them. A 16px-radius card with 8px padding wants an 8px-radius inner element. Matching the inner radius to the outer produces a visible gap at the corner — the most common radius error, and it is fully determinable at design time.

BORDER WIDTH SCALE:
`border/none` 0 · `border/thin` 1 · `border/medium` 2 · `border/thick` 4
Note that 1px hairlines are not 1 physical pixel on high-DPI screens, and a 0.5px border is a legitimate iOS convention (list separators) that does not translate to the web.

FOCUS RING — this deserves its own token group because it is a WCAG requirement and it is routinely improvised:
- `focus/width` 2px minimum
- `focus/offset` 2px, so the ring reads as separate from the element's own border
- `focus/colour` a dedicated semantic token, NOT the brand primary. It needs 3:1 against BOTH the element and the surrounding surface, which a brand colour usually fails on at least one of.
- `focus/style` solid outline. Prefer `outline` over `box-shadow` so it survives forced-colours / high-contrast mode.
A two-tone ring (a light inner and dark outer, or a 2px ring with a 1px white offset) is the only pattern that reliably meets 3:1 on both light and dark surfaces without a per-surface token.

WHAT MUST NEVER SHIP: `outline: none` with no replacement. It is the single most common accessibility failure on the web and it is a design-system-level fix — put the focus treatment inside the component so it cannot be omitted downstream.

STROKE VS BORDER IN FIGMA: Figma strokes can be inside, centre, or outside. Only INSIDE matches CSS `border` box behaviour. Centre and outside strokes change the element's visual size relative to its frame and will not match the build.

title: Token Set Completeness — What a Finished Foundation Contains
content:
Most token sets stop at colour, spacing, and type, and then every other value is improvised in components forever. This is the full checklist.

CORE (almost always present)
- COLOUR — primitive ramps, semantic roles, component tokens, per mode
- SPACING — scale plus semantics (inset/stack/inline/gap, see dsf-001)
- TYPOGRAPHY — families, size scale, weights, line heights, letter spacing, composite text styles

ROUTINELY MISSING
- ELEVATION — shadow levels AND the dark-mode equivalent (surface lightness, since shadows are near-invisible on dark)
- Z-INDEX / LAYERING — see dsf-004
- BORDER — width scale, radius scale, nested-radius rule
- FOCUS — width, offset, colour, style. Its own group, not borrowed from border
- MOTION — duration scale, easing curves, reduced-motion overrides (see figma-prototyping-lore ms-002, ms-003)
- OPACITY — a small scale for disabled, overlays, scrims, hover washes
- ICON — size ramp bound to the icon system
- BREAKPOINT — the values themselves as tokens, so grid and type modes can reference them
- CONTAINER / MEASURE — max content widths and the text measure cap (independent of container)
- DENSITY — a mode that remaps spacing semantics one step
- TOUCH TARGET — minimums as tokens so they can be enforced, not remembered
- DURATION-ADJACENT — transition delays and stagger intervals if you choreograph

THE COMPLETENESS TEST: open any three finished components and list every numeric or colour value in them. Every value that does not resolve to a token is either a missing token or a deliberate exception. Deliberate exceptions should be countable on one hand.

THE ORDER TO BUILD IN: colour and spacing first (they touch everything), then typography, then border and radius, then elevation and focus, then motion, then the long tail. Building the long tail early produces tokens nobody uses; building it never produces components full of magic numbers.
